catalog_quote: A phonological word in Dadibi consists of one obligatory nuclear syllable with a high or low tone and from zero to 6 marginal syllables. 3.1 Description When the nuclear syllable of the word is high tone, it has extra intensity (sometimes very slight). High nuclear tones tend to pull following pitches to high and the words have a very quick tempo. When a low tone falls on the nuclear syllable, it has extra length. Low nuclear syllables tend to pull following pitches toward low, and the words are much slower in tempo. Preceding syllables tend to fluctuate. ... The contrastive intensity of the nuclear syllable seems to be of more importance than the correct tone on that syllable. However, by knowing the correct nuclear tone one is able to determine the appropriate tempo, the overall pitch and rhythm ... 3.2.2 Two syllable words: High on the first syllable contrasts with high on the second…

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Quote confirmed verbatim at the stated pages in the SIL scan we hold (scanned + page image). The deciding source is the dedicated primary phonology (MacDonald & MacDonald 1974), which is the best and essentially only description of Dadibi prosody; Glottolog lists no competing phonology and web search found no later instrumental/phonological work. Two open items downloaded now — MacDonald's 1992 Organised Phonology Data (primary, same minimal pairs, two contrastive tones on one syllable per word) and Cahill 2011 (secondary survey explicitly equating the nuclear tone-bearing syllable with stress, position lexically contrastive) — both confirm the 'tonal (culminative word-tone), no independent positional stress rule' coding. Only unheld descriptive work is the 1976 UPNG MA grammar (print only), unlikely to change anything.

sources.quote: 'there is only one syllable on the word which bears contrastive tone, and this may be called the stressed syllable (MacDonald and MacDonald label it the "nuclear syllable"). ... A High tone has extra intensity ... A Low tone lengthens the nuclear syllable' — classed with Fasu/Kairi as word tone with one tone-bearing (stressed) syllable whose position is contrastive (káli vs kalí). Secondary, based on MacDonald & MacDonald 1974.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'There are two contrasting tones: high tone and low tone. wà 'string bag' / wá 'edible greens'; káli 'kaukau' / kalí 'tree type'; kebá 'axe' / kebà 'canoe'; àga 'his' / agà 'his own'.' Tone marked on one syllable per word; 'Phonemic tone is not written' (orthography). No separate stress rule given.
